topic.title: Translating an Oxygen User Manual with Content Fusion
topic.shortdesc: How we used the AI translation agent in Content Fusion to translate the Content Fusion Cloud user manual into French, and what we learned about getting a translation that matches the product.

body.p: In The Translation Workflow for the AI Era, we introduced the AI translation workflow in Content Fusion.
In this post, we share our experience with translating the Content Fusion Cloud user manual into French.

image.alt: The translation resources guide every job. Each release goes through branch, translate, check, AI review, expert review, and publish.

ol.li: Create a translation branch: keep the translation work apart from the source content.
Prepare the translation resources: give the agent the product's UI strings and the approved terminology.
Translate: run a translation job and bring its results into your workspace.
Review the translation: check the result with a quick check, a bilingual reviewer, and an AI review.
Integrate and publish: merge the translation branch and publish the translated manual.

section.title: Before you begin
section.p: You need:

ul.li: Access to the User Guide project in Content Fusion, with permission to create branches.
AI credits in your Content Fusion organization. A translation job stops when the credits run out.
A local clone of the User Guide repository, to update the UI strings (see Get the latest UI strings).

body.p: Do all the translation work on a dedicated Git branch. The branch keeps the translated files apart from the source content. This matters during the review: the reviewer compares each translated topic with its English source, and the source must not change while they do it. When the translation is approved, you merge the branch back.

ol.li: In Content Fusion, open the User Guide project.
Make sure you are in your personal workspace, not in a review task.
In the top stripe, click the branch drop-down menu, then select Create new branch....

Enter the name of the new branch. Use this pattern: translation/translate--<product-name>--<lang>
<product-name>: the product name, with hyphens instead of spaces.
<lang>: the target language as a BCP 47 tag.
Example: translation/translate--Content-Fusion-Cloud--fr-FR
Select the branch to start from: the branch that holds the English content you want to translate.

body.note: Before you continue, check that the top stripe shows the translation branch. Everything you do from now on is saved on this branch.
body.p: For more about branches, see Branch Management in the Oxygen Content Fusion User Guide.
A general-purpose translation is rarely good enough for a user manual. Two things make the difference:

ul.li: Every menu, button, and dialog name in the text matches what the reader sees on screen.
Every product concept is translated the same way in every topic.

body.p: The agent does not know these rules by itself. You give them to it in a few files, before you translate.

section.title: Where the agent finds the project rules
section.p: The agent reads the project rules from .contentfusion/i18n/agent-instructions.md and applies them to every translation job, on top of its built-in rules. For one-time requests, use the Translation Instructions field of the job instead.

For the Oxygen user manuals, the project rules are split across three files in .contentfusion/i18n/. agent-instructions.md holds the general rules. The two large lists, the UI strings and the terminology, have their own file for each product and language. The agent loads only the lists that the current job needs:

row.entry: The rules for every translation, the list of products, and how to use the next two files.
The product's translated UI labels and messages.
The approved translation of each product concept, and the terms that stay in English.

section.p: In these paths, <product> is the product's resource folder (fusion for Content Fusion) and <lang> is the BCP 47 tag with an underscore (fr_FR).

section.title: UI strings and terminology: what is the difference?
section.p: Both files tell the agent which words to use, but in different ways:

ul.li: A UI string is copied exactly. The reader must find it on screen, so the agent never changes it. If the label does not fit the grammar of the sentence, the agent rewrites the sentence around the label.
A term is adapted to the sentence. It fixes which word to use for a concept, but the word can change its form: singular or plural, with or without an article, and so on.

section.title: UI strings
section.p: UI strings are the texts that the product displays: menus, options, buttons, view and dialog names, and messages. For example, the New project action or the Task activity section.
The UI strings file is a table generated from the product's own translation files. Each row gives a string's ID, its English text, its translation, and where it appears:
section.codeblock: | ID | Source (en-US) | Target (fr_FR) | Context | |---|---|---|---| | save | Save | Enregistrer | Save button label; Generic save button text | | activity | Task activity | Activité de tâche | Section title for the activity stream related to a task. |
section.p: The agent uses the Target text exactly as it is. These French examples show why:

row.entry: The Task activity section lists the comments.
La section Activité de la tâche affiche les commentaires.
La section Activité de tâche affiche les commentaires.

section.p: Each wrong translation reads well, but the reader cannot find the label on screen.

section.title: Terminology
section.p: The terminology file holds the concepts of the product and its domain, such as DITA map, transformation scenario, or Git repository. It has two tables.
The Terms table gives the approved translation of each concept. The Details column adds the grammar the agent needs (part of speech, gender), the translations to avoid, and example sentences:
section.codeblock: | Source | Target | Context | Details | |---|---|---|---| | workspace | espace de travail | user's working copy of a project | pos: noun; gender: m; ex: from a card in your workspace → depuis une fiche de votre espace de travail | | review task | tâche de révision | unit of review work in Content Fusion | pos: noun; gender: f; deprecated: tâche d'examen; deprecated: tâche de revue |
section.p: The agent always uses the approved word, but adapts its form to the sentence:

row.entry: The review tasks are listed in your workspace.
Les tâches de révision sont listées dans votre espace de travail.
Fermez toutes les tâches de révision.

section.p: The Do not translate table lists the terms that stay in English: product and brand names, acronyms, file names, and code. The Note column tells the agent how the term behaves in the target language:
section.codeblock: | Term | Kind | Note | |---|---|---| | Content Fusion | product | short product name | | DITA map | name | feminine in French (la DITA map), plural DITA maps; map alone → carte |
section.p: For example, Open the DITA map. becomes Ouvrez la DITA map., not Ouvrez la carte DITA.

section.title: Check the resources before you translate
section.p: The terminology file is maintained by hand. The UI strings file is generated, and it gets out of date when the product changes. Before each translation:

ol.li: Get the latest UI strings and convert them to Markdown.
Register the product, if this is its first translation.
Get the latest XML UI strings for the product. Follow the instructions on the Oxygen i18n wiki page.

Save the XML files in translation/xml-translation/<product>/.
Example: translation/xml-translation/fusion/

topic.title: Convert the UI strings to Markdown

body.p: The agent reads the UI strings as a Markdown table, not as XML. The translation/ui-strings-to-md.xsl stylesheet converts them. It writes one ui-strings.<lang>.md file for each language in the XML files.
Run it in one of two ways:

ul.li: Option A: Run the script. Needs Java 11 or later and Saxon-HE 12.
Option B: Run the stylesheet in Oxygen XML Editor. Nothing to install: Oxygen XML Editor includes Saxon.

ol.li:
Open the script in a text editor:
Windows: translation\ui-strings-to-md.bat
Linux, macOS, or Git Bash: translation/ui-strings-to-md.sh

In the Settings section at the top of the script, check these variables. Relative paths start from the translation folder.
IN_DIR: the folder with the XML UI strings.
Example: xml-translation/fusion
OUT_DIR: the product's terminology folder.
Example: ../.contentfusion/i18n/fusion/terminology
SAXON_LIB: leave it empty if Saxon-HE 12 is in your local Maven repository (~/.m2/repository). Otherwise, set it to the Saxon-HE 12 folder (the folder with the Saxon jar and its lib/ subfolder).

Run the script.
Windows:translation\ui-strings-to-md.bat
Linux, macOS, or Git Bash:translation/ui-strings-to-md.sh
If the script stops with an ERROR: line, fix the cause and run it again. Usually, Java or Saxon is not found, or the input folder is wrong.
Check the diff of the Markdown files, then commit them.

topic.title: Option B: Run the stylesheet in Oxygen XML Editor

ol.li: In Oxygen XML Editor, open translation/ui-strings-to-md.xsl.

Create a transformation scenario:
Select Configure Transformation Scenario(s), then New XSLT transformation .
Leave the XML URL field empty.
Set Transformer to Saxon-HE, PE, or EE, version 12 or later.
In the Saxon advanced options, set Initial template to xsl:initial-template.

Click Parameters and set these parameters. Relative paths start from the translation folder.
in: the folder with the XML UI strings.
Example: xml-translation/fusion/
out: the product's terminology folder.
Example: ../.contentfusion/i18n/fusion/terminology/

Apply the scenario.
The Markdown files are written to the out folder. Warnings about missing translations appear in the Results panel.
Check the diff of the Markdown files, then commit them.

body.p: The agent finds the product's resource folder in the Products table of .contentfusion/i18n/agent-instructions.md. If the product is already in the table, skip this task.
Otherwise, add a row with the product name and its <product> folder:
body.note: When you start the translation job, name the product exactly as it appears in this table. If the agent does not find the product in the table, it stops before it translates anything.

body.p: The agent translates only the files that need it. For each source file, it checks the translation index (.contentfusion/i18n/translation-index.xml) and finds one of three states:

ul.li: Missing: the file was never translated into this language. The agent translates it.

Stale: the English source changed after the last translation. The agent translates it again, and uses the existing translation as context, so the earlier wording and your manual corrections are kept where they still apply.
Current: the translation matches the English source. The agent skips it.

body.p: That is why you can run this step again at any time to update a translation.

section.title: Start the translation job

ol.li: In Content Fusion, open the User Guide project, and check that the translation branch is selected in the top stripe.

Click New translation, and set these fields:
Publications: the publication of the manual to translate.
Target Languages: one or more target languages.
Translation Instructions: the product name, exactly as it appears in the Products table, and the folder for the translated files.
Example:Translations are for product: `Content Fusion`.
Save translations to `DITA-cf/i18n/fusion-cloud/fr-FR/`, mirroring the source structure inside it.
Click Start translation.

section.note: To translate into several languages, select all of them in one job. The job translates them one after another.

section.title: The first translation into a language
section.p: The first job for a language also creates the translation index entries, the translated maps, a copy of every image, and the deliverables for the new language. It copies the deliverables that already exist for English. See The First Time You Translate a Project in the Oxygen Content Fusion User Guide.

section.title: Follow the job
section.p: The job appears as a card in your workspace. The card shows the current step and the progress. You can stop the job from the card.
section.note: While the job runs, do not change the source files or the translated files that it covers. Your changes can conflict with the files that the agent writes.
section.p: If the job fails, click View log on the card to see the cause. For example, the job fails when your organization runs out of AI credits. If the job produced some files before it failed, select Bring partial results into workspace to keep them. To run the same job again, select Re-run from the card's menu.
For more, see Managing a Translation Job in the Oxygen Content Fusion User Guide.

section.title: Bring the translation into your workspace

ol.li: When the job finishes, click Bring into workspace on the card. The translated files and the updated translation index are added to your workspace as uncommitted changes.
Check what the job changed.

Commit the files to the translation branch.
A reviewer can open the translated files only after you commit them.

body.p: Use any of these methods to review the translation. Each one finds different problems, so combine them when you can.

row.entry: Unexpected files, invalid DITA, broken references.
Wrong terms and UI labels, inconsistencies, missing text, in every topic.

body.p: When you find a problem, fix it at its cause. See Fix the issues.

section.title: Check what the job changed
section.p: Do this check right after you bring the translation into your workspace, before you commit it.

ul.li: Changes view: lists every file the job added or modified: the translated topics, the translation index, and, for a new language, the deliverables. Make sure the job changed only the files you expected. The English topics must not be in the list.
Problems view: shows validation errors. Make sure the translated publication is valid DITA and has no broken references.

section.p: For details, see Reviewing Translations Before You Commit in the Oxygen Content Fusion User Guide.

section.title: Review with an AI agent
section.p: A human reviewer rarely reads every topic of a large manual. An AI agent can. The translation/review-prompt.md file is a review prompt written for the Oxygen user manuals. It tells the agent to compare every translated topic with its source and to look for these problems:

ul.li: Terminology: a term that does not use its approved translation.
UI terminology: a menu, button, or dialog name that does not match the product's UI strings.
Language quality: grammar, spelling, and the typography of the target language, such as the non-breaking space before a colon in French.
Accuracy and completeness: text that is missing, added, or that changes the meaning of the source.
Consistency: the same concept translated in different ways in different topics.
Style and naturalness: text that reads like a translation, not like a manual written in the target language.

section.p: You run the review as a translation job that does not translate anything. The agent only reads the files and writes a report.

ol.li: In Content Fusion, open the User Guide project, and check that the translation branch is selected in the top stripe.

Click New translation, and set these fields:
Publications: the translated publication.
Target Languages: the language to review.
Translation Instructions: tell the agent not to translate, to follow the review prompt, and which language to review. Write the language tag exactly as it appears in the translation index.
Example:Do not translate anything. Follow the instructions in `translation/review-prompt.md`, with TARGET_LANG = fr-FR.

Click Start translation.
The agent finds the translated topics in the translation index and uses the same project rules as the translation agent. It writes the report to translation-review-<lang>.md at the root of the repository.
When the job finishes, click Bring into workspace on the card, then open the report.

Start with the Root-cause rollup table at the top of the report. A few root causes usually explain most issues, and the table tells you where to fix each one. Then read the issue records: each one shows the source text, the current translation, and a recommended translation.

section.p: You can ask the agent other questions in the same way. See Asking the Agent a Question in the Oxygen Content Fusion User Guide.

section.title: Ask a translation expert
section.p: A reviewer who knows both languages is the best judge of meaning and style. The reviewer reads each translated topic side by side with its English source, in one of these tools:

ul.li: Content Fusion: with the translation branch selected, create a project review task that includes the translated topics, and invite the reviewer. The reviewer edits the topics or adds comments in the browser. When the review is done, you integrate the accepted changes into the translation branch. See Creating a Project Review Task.

Oxygen XML Editor: the reviewer checks out the translation branch and reviews the files locally. This suits reviewers who prefer a desktop editor, or who want the source and the translation open side by side.

section.note: Attach the English PDF of the manual to the review task, so the reviewer sees each topic in its context.

section.title: Fix the issues
section.p: Where you fix an issue depends on its cause:

row.entry: A one-time mistake in a single topic
The translated topic. Edit it directly.
Commit the change. Later translation jobs skip the topic and keep your correction, as long as its English source does not change.
A wrong or missing term or UI string, or a rule that the agent did not follow
The terminology file, the UI strings file, or agent-instructions.md.
An error or unclear text in the English source
The English topic, on the translation branch. The fix reaches the source branch when you integrate the translation branch.
The topic becomes stale, and the next job translates it again. Fix the source only after the review is complete, so the reviewers compare the translation with the source it was made from.

section.title: Retranslate after you change the rules
section.p: A change in the terminology, the UI strings, or agent-instructions.md does not make a translation stale. The agent tracks only changes in the English source, so the next job skips the topics that are already translated. To make the agent translate them again, remove their entries from the translation index:

ol.li: Open .contentfusion/i18n/translation-index.xml.
Delete the entries for the topics you want to retranslate. The topics become missing, so the next job translates them again.
Commit your changes, then run the translation again.
Review the retranslated topics.

section.note: The next job overwrites the translated topics whose entries you deleted. If you corrected some of them by hand, commit the corrections before you run the job, so you can restore them.
section.p: When the review finds no more important issues, continue with Integrate and publish.

body.p: When the review is complete, merge the translation branch back into the branch you created it from. The merge brings the translated files, the updated translation index, and any source fixes from the review.

ol.li: In Content Fusion, select the target branch in the top stripe.
From the branch drop-down menu, select Merge into current branch..., then select the translation branch.
Optional: publish the translated manual from the project's Deliverables page. The first translation job created the deliverables for the new language.

body.p: For details, see Branch Management in the Oxygen Content Fusion User Guide.
body.note: Mark the release with a Git tag. A tag records the exact commit of each translation release, so you can later compare two releases, or rebuild the manual exactly as it was published.
